uncited: Blurpool Resampling is a differentiable resampling method used in neural volume rendering to generate new sample positions ($t$ values) along rays based on a learned or estimated weight distribution.
It solves the problem of adapting sample density to scene complexity by treating the sampling process as a differentiable operation on a discrete probability distribution.
It sets itself apart from [Max Dilation](8984-max-dilation.md) by using average pooling on max-pooled weights to create a smoother, blurrier distribution, whereas Max Dilation uses only max-pooling.
It builds on [Step Function Resampling](8985-step-function-resampling.md) by providing the specific weight transformation logic required before sampling.
The method transforms input weights associated with initial sample positions into a new set of sample positions.
It operates on a piecewise constant probability density function (PDF) derived from the weights.
*   **Input Weights**: Tensor of shape `[batch_size, num_samples]`.
Represents the importance or probability mass of each initial sample.
*   **Output t_samples**: Tensor of shape `[batch_size, num_samples + 1]`.
*   **Output Points**: Tensor of shape `[batch_size, num_samples, 3]`.
The core data structure is the weight tensor.
The algorithm assumes the weights define a discrete distribution over the initial sample indices.
The output `t_samples` defines the boundaries of the new intervals, implying `num_samples + 1` boundaries for `num_samples` intervals.
**Padding**: Pad the input weights tensor `weights` of shape `[B, N]` along the last dimension.
Concatenate the first element, the original weights, and the last element.
**Max Pooling**: Compute the element-wise maximum of adjacent elements in `weights_pad`.
**Blurpool (Average Pooling)**: Compute the element-wise average of adjacent elements in `weights_max`.
**Add Padding**: Add the `resample_padding` scalar to `weights_blur`.
**Sampling**: Sample new $t$ values from the normalized distribution defined by `weights_final`.
This is done using a sorted piecewise constant PDF sampler.
**Ray Casting**: Cast rays using the new $t$ values, ray origins, directions, and radii to compute the mean positions and covariances.
*   **Zero Weights**: If all weights are zero, normalization fails.
*   **Precision**: Floating-point precision issues in cumulative sum and inverse CDF sampling can lead to incorrect sample positions.
*   **Time Complexity**: $O(N)$ per ray, where $N$ is the number of samples.
The operations are element-wise tensor operations.
*   **Memory Complexity**: $O(N)$ for storing intermediate tensors (`weights_pad`, `weights_max`, `weights_blur`).
Smooths the weight distribution, potentially leading to more stable sampling.
*   **Limitations**: The blurpool operation may oversmooth sharp peaks in the weight distribution, leading to less accurate sampling in high-detail regions compared to non-smoothed methods.
*   **When to Use**: When differentiable sampling is required and a smooth weight distribution is beneficial.
*   **When Not to Use**: When sharp, precise sampling is needed and differentiability is not required.

Blurpool Resampling is used in neural volume rendering frameworks, specifically in implementations like [AlexSheldrick/density_bounded_ray_weights](https://github.com/AlexSheldrick/density_bounded_ray_weights) and [CPREgroup/CaSE-NeRF](https://github.com/CPREgroup/CaSE-NeRF).
It is an adaptation of the "blurpool" concept from image processing (used in convolutional neural networks to reduce aliasing) to the domain of ray sampling.
The method was introduced in unofficial repositories as part of efforts to improve the stability and quality of NeRF training by adapting sample densities.
